--- title: "Data and models" description: "The datasets, targets and models used in every example." --- ## French motor insurance (freMTPL2) The dataset comes from a French insurer and is published on [OpenML](https://www.openml.org/d/41214) in two tables: one row per policy (risk features and exposure) and one row per claim (claim amount). It contains 678\,013 policies. | Feature | Description | |---|---| | `Area`, `Region` | Where the policyholder lives | | `Density` | Inhabitants per km² in the policyholder's city | | `DrivAge` | Age of the driver | | `BonusMalus` | Bonus-malus level: below 100 means a claim-free history, above 100 a surcharge | | `VehPower`, `VehAge`, `VehBrand`, `VehGas` | Vehicle power, age, brand and fuel | | `Exposure` | Fraction of a year the policy was in force (≤ 1) | ### Targets **`HasClaim` (binary).** 1 if the policy had at least one claim during its exposure period, 0 otherwise. Only 3\.7% of policies had a claim, so the classes are heavily imbalanced, which is typical for real classification problems and important for how metrics behave. **`PurePremium` (continuous).** Total claim cost divided by exposure, i.e. the cost per policy-year. It's what an insurer has to charge (before expenses) to cover claims. 96\.3% of policies have a pure premium of 0, and the rest have a long right tail. Because pure premium is a rate per year, a policy observed for a full year carries more information than one observed for a week. All pure-premium models and metrics are therefore **weighted by exposure**. ::: {.callout-note} ## Data preparation - The claim count is taken from the claims table, so `HasClaim` and `PurePremium` always agree. - Total claim cost per policy is capped at 200\,000 EUR (a few claims reach 4 million), and exposure is capped at 1 year. - Average cost per claim ('severity') was considered as a target and dropped: in this dataset, no model predicts it better than the overall mean. ::: ::: {#tbl-targets .cell tbl-cap='Distribution of the two targets.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} pp = policies.loc[policies["PurePremium"] > 0, "PurePremium"] pd.DataFrame( { "Statistic": ["Policies", "Claim rate", "Share with pure premium 0", "Median pure premium (when > 0)", "99th percentile (when > 0)"], "Value": [n_policies, claim_rate, share_zero, f"{pp.median():,.0f} EUR", f"{pp.quantile(0.99):,.0f} EUR"], } ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
Statistic Value
0 Policies 678,013
1 Claim rate 3.7%
2 Share with pure premium 0 96.3%
3 Median pure premium (when > 0) 1,504 EUR
4 99th percentile (when > 0) 110,889 EUR
``` ::: ::: ### Train/test split Policies are split once into 75% training and 25% test data (169\,504 policies), stratified on `HasClaim` so both parts have the same claim rate. **Every metric in this project is computed on the test set.** Performance on the training data says how well a model memorized it, not how it will perform on new policies. ## California Housing A classic regression dataset (shipped with scikit-learn): the median house value of 20,640 Californian districts from the 1990 census, in units of 100,000 USD, with 8 features such as median income, house age and location. Unlike pure premium, it has a strong, smooth signal, so we use it to show how error metrics behave in the textbook case. It has one quirk: values were capped at 5.0 when the data was collected, which shows up in the residual plots. ## Models Every target gets the same three models: | Model | `HasClaim` | `PurePremium` | California Housing | |---|---|---|---| | **Null** | training claim rate | training mean (exposure-weighted) | training mean | | **GLM** | logistic regression | Tweedie GLM, power 1.9, log link | linear regression | | **GBM** | gradient boosting, log loss | gradient boosting, Poisson loss | gradient boosting, squared error | - **Null** is the 'no model' reference. Any metric value only means something next to what the Null model achieves. - **GLM** is the traditional, interpretable baseline, still the standard in insurance pricing. The insurance GLMs use one-hot encoded categoricals, binned vehicle and driver age, and log-scaled density and bonus-malus. - **GBM** (`HistGradientBoosting` in scikit-learn) is the flexible challenger. It handles the categorical features natively and stops adding trees when a validation split stops improving. The models are deliberately reasonable but not heavily tuned: the project is about *measuring* performance, not maximizing it. ::: {#tbl-predictions .cell tbl-cap='Average test-set prediction of each model next to the actual average.' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} b, p, h = binary_predictions(), pure_premium_predictions(), housing_predictions() rows = { "HasClaim (claim rate)": [b["y"].mean()] + [b[m].mean() for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")], "PurePremium (EUR/year)": [np.average(p["y"], weights=p["w"])] + [np.average(p[m], weights=p["w"]) for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")], "House value (100k USD)": [h["y"].mean()] + [h[m].mean() for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")], } pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["Actual", "Null", "GLM", "GBM"]).T.round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
Actual Null GLM GBM
HasClaim (claim rate) 0.0368 0.0368 0.0366 0.0367
PurePremium (EUR/year) 146.3359 145.3345 145.1925 142.6470
House value (100k USD) 2.0632 2.0703 2.0620 2.0729
``` ::: ::: Here is how to get these predictions in your own code: ::: {#11cbec8b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} from modelperf.models import binary_predictions b = binary_predictions() # columns: y, Null, GLM, GBM (one row per test policy) ``` :::
